questions.q: What is the smallest deployable unit in Kubernetes?
options: A container
A Pod
A Node
A Deployment
questions.explain: Kubernetes schedules Pods, not individual containers. A Pod wraps one or more containers that are always scheduled together.

questions.q: What do all containers within the same Pod share?
options: Nothing — each container is fully isolated
A network namespace (one IP, one port space) and any defined storage volumes
Only CPU limits, not network
A shared database connection
questions.explain: Containers in the same Pod share one IP address and port space, communicating over localhost, and can share mounted volumes for file access.

questions.q: When is a multi-container Pod the right design choice?
options: Whenever you want to group two unrelated services together to save resources
When a helper process, like a log shipper, needs to start/stop with the main container and share its network — tight coupling
Every Pod should have multiple containers by default
Only for StatefulSets
questions.explain: Multi-container Pods are reserved for genuinely tight coupling, like sidecars that need to share the main container's lifecycle and network — not a general-purpose grouping mechanism.

questions.q: A Pod's node crashes. What happens to that Pod?
options: Kubernetes restarts the exact same Pod with the same name and IP once the node recovers
The Pod is gone; a replacement Pod is scheduled elsewhere with a new name and often a new IP
The Pod moves itself to a different node automatically, keeping its identity
Nothing — Pods cannot be replaced once created
questions.explain: Pods are disposable: a failed Pod is not restarted in place. A new Pod with a new identity gets scheduled, which is why nothing should depend on a specific Pod's identity surviving.

questions.q: Why do you almost never create a Pod directly with `kubectl apply -f pod.yaml` in practice?
options: Because kubectl cannot create Pods directly
Because a directly-created Pod isn't managed by a controller, so nothing replaces it if its node fails
Because Pods require a Service to exist first
Because Pod YAML is deprecated
questions.explain: A bare Pod has no controller watching over it — if it or its node fails, nothing recreates it. Higher-level controllers like Deployments manage a set of Pods and recreate them automatically.
